title: Maskless wafer-flash interference lattice with a coarse cut mask
idea: Expose the entire wafer's capacitor-hole lattice in one flash with three-beam 193 nm laser interference (hexagonal pattern, no mask, no projection lens), reach final pitch by self-aligned pitch splitting, and erase the lattice outside the arrays with a cheap KrF keep/cut mask.
why: An interference rig is <$5M versus ~$200M EUV, and a wafer-scale flash takes seconds instead of ~100 field exposures (Fact 4).

title: Backside-power analogy: deep-trench capacitors etched from wafer backside
idea: Borrowed from logic backside power delivery and BSI image sensors: build transistors and bitlines on the front, bond to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, then etch deep-trench storage capacitors from the backside, landing on each transistor's source through nano-TSVs, so capacitors stop competing with bitline contacts for front-side space.
why: Facts 1/7: capacitor height is decoupled from front topology and the front area is freed for periphery; nano-TSV alignment at ~30 nm pitch is high risk.

title: Pharmaceutical isolators: a ballroom-free DRAM fab
idea: Pharma replaced Grade-A cleanroom suites with sealed isolators; keep ISO-1 air only inside FOUPs, EFEMs and tool minienvironments, run the building at ISO-8, and give every tool maintenance access through pharma-style rapid-transfer ports (alpha/beta double doors) so the tool interior is never exposed to room air.
why: Fab capital, energy and build time: cleanroom shell plus HVAC is ~15-25% of fab construction cost; claim 10-15% capex and 20-30% facility-energy reduction and a faster build.

title: Stem-cell wafers: one front-end mask set, differentiated in last metals
idea: Stem cells differentiate on signal; run one universal array-plus-periphery front end for DDR5, LPDDR, HBM base and CXL parts, then personalize I/O, bank grouping and density bin in the last two metal layers by maskless e-beam or laser direct write.
why: Cuts mask sets across a product family ~4x (EUV sets cost $10-20M) and lets WIP swing between products within days; est. 10-15% better capex utilization.

title: Lending library: used-DUV-only DRAM fab wins density by stacking
idea: Random stimulus 'library' (reuse old books) -> a U.S. fab is built from refurbished ArF immersion scanners and depreciated etch/dep tools at F~18-20 nm using SAQP. The lost density is recovered with a 4F2 vertical-channel cell plus two hybrid-bonded array layers, so the fab needs zero EUV.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: used 193i tools cost ~$20-40M versus $200-400M per EUV scanner. Equal bits per mm2 could come at roughly 40% lower fab capex and with no export-controlled tools.

title: Mask-free interference lithography for every periodic array layer
idea: First principle: a DRAM array is a lattice whose whole information content is one unit cell plus two lattice vectors (~100 bits), yet each array layer goes through a $300k+ EUV mask and a ~$200M projection scanner. Print the active, wordline, bitline and storage-node-contact layers with a reticle-free 4-beam 193i (or EUV) interference stepper that has no projection optics, and trim the array edges with one coarse DUV block mask, so masks are needed only for the periphery.
why: Litho capital and masks (fact 4): an interference tool costs ~1/5-1/10 as much as a scanner per wafer-pass and removes 3-5 EUV array exposures; claimed ~20-30% lower wafer cost.

title: Scanner-hour exchange: rent idle logic-fab EUV for DRAM layers
idea: Constraint: the DRAM fab may buy zero EUV scanners. A brokered exchange sells logic foundries' EUV utilization dips; DRAM lots travel in sealed FOUPs to a nearby logic fab for 2-3 critical exposures under a standardized resist/track recipe, then return.
why: Fact 4 capital: avoids $400M+ of scanners per DRAM fab, lifts industry EUV utilization 10-15%, and makes U.S. DRAM fabs viable next to Arizona/Texas logic fabs.

title: Self-aligned octuple patterning lets old 193i scanners print 1x-nm
idea: Po: the old scanner prints finer than its spec. Add three generations of spacer cascades (SAOP) to a 2x-nm DRAM line's existing 193i scanners so an 80 nm litho pitch becomes 10 nm lines for wordlines/bitlines; only extra ALD and etch chambers go into the existing building.
why: EUV dependence and capital: lifts an old fab ~1.5-2 nodes in density without EUV for ~10% of new-fab cost.

title: O: downstream atomic-oxygen ash ends sulfuric-peroxide resist strips
idea: Strip implant and patterning resists with a remote O-radical plasma preceded by an H2/N2 radical crust-break step, eliminating hot sulfuric-peroxide (SPM) baths and their rinses.
why: Water and chemicals: SPM strips and hot rinses are heavy UPW and acid users; dry strip cuts that module's water >10x and removes sulfuric waste treatment.

title: Online CVD on hot float-glass ribbon deposits memory blanket layers
idea: Worse: deposit every blanket film in a $5M vacuum chamber, one substrate at a time. Flip: as float glass leaves the tin bath at ~600 C, apply atmospheric online CVD (already used for pyrolytic low-E coatings) to lay down barrier, bottom-electrode and oxide-semiconductor blanket layers at kilometers per day, then cut panels for patterning.
why: Throughput/capital: blanket deposition cost per m2 ~100x lower, using existing U.S. float lines.

title: Eliminate scrap from partial dies: sell them as JEDEC 24Gb parts
idea: Design 32 Gb DDR5 dies so any one quarter of the array can be fused off; dies with a dead quadrant are configured as the non-binary 24 Gb density already in the DDR5 spec and built into standard 24/48/96 GB modules that hosts already support.
why: Yield and capital: recovers ~5-15% of dies that would be scrapped during a ramp, adding effective wafer capacity without a single new tool.

title: Float-glass analog: silicon ribbon floated on molten metal
idea: Borrowed from Pilkington's float-glass process: pull a thin single-crystal silicon ribbon horizontally from a seed across a denser molten Sn-based bath under a barrier skin, producing 300 mm-wide wafer-thick sheet with no quartz crucible and no wire sawing, then grow a device-grade epi layer on top.
why: Scarce resource and cost: removes Spruce Pine HPQ crucibles and ~40% kerf loss; continuous growth could halve substrate cost. Metal contamination and crystal quality are high risk.

title: Reusable capacitor-forest template: grow once, transfer-print many times
idea: First principle: the costly high-AR etch only defines a shape, and a shape can be reused if the mold separates cleanly. Etch one master Si template with high-AR pores, grow capacitor electrodes plus high-k inside a release liner, transfer-bond the capacitor forest onto the storage-node contacts, and lift the template off for 50-100 reuses.
why: Capacitor etch capex (fact 1): the hardest etch is amortized over many wafers; the template is reused by design.

title: Contract-brewing program: idle U.S. fabs add BEOL memory layers
idea: As craft brewers rent others' tanks, a federal tolling program buys finished CMOS periphery wafers from foundries and pays idle U.S. 200/300 mm fabs per wafer to add DUV-only, <=350 C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell memory layers, with 5-year guaranteed offtake.
why: U.S. manufacturability/capital: reuses depreciated tools and staff with no EUV and no new shell; output in ~18 months vs 3-5 years for a new fab.

title: Electroless ruthenium wordlines and plugs escape tungsten and WF6
idea: Box: standard cell x buried-wordline access with Ru gate fill x standard sensing x 2D x Si x seedless electroless or ALD-seeded Ru plating. Buried wordlines and contact plugs, today CVD W from WF6, are filled bottom-up by barrier-free Ru (short electron mean free path keeps resistivity low in 10 nm trenches).
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and fluorine chemistry removed; barrier-free fill gives ~30% lower WL RC or allows a thinner WL that lowers GIDL; Ru needed is micrograms per die.

title: Ball Semiconductor's sealed-flow, cleanroom-free fab applied to flat memory wafers
idea: Ball Semiconductor proposed processing 1 mm silicon spheres in sealed tubes without a cleanroom and failed because lithography on spheres was poor. Keep the part that worked, sealed continuously flowing minienvironments, but carry flat wafers in nitrogen-purged pods through linked single-wafer modules so DRAM's repetitive flow needs no ballroom cleanroom.
why: Fab cost: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of capex and much of a fab's water and energy; claims ~25% capex cut and an 18-month build.

title: Wafer-scale memory plate: one undiced wafer per rack sled
idea: Shift the product unit from die up to whole wafer: stitched identical array fields with redundant inter-field links, no dicing, no per-die packaging; the 300 mm wafer is mounted on a cooled sled board with edge connectors as a ~1-2 TB rack memory plate that routes around dead fields at boot.
why: Deletes dicing, packaging and per-die known-good-die test (~15-25% of finished DRAM cost) plus ~5% scribe area; I/O periphery is shared across fields.

title: Twin tunnel-diode latch grown where the capacitor used to be
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging joins storage and restoring in one element: epitaxially stack two Si/SiGe interband tunnel diodes in a short ~5:1 hole above the access transistor; their negative-differential-resistance curves cross at two stable node voltages, and with sub-pA peak current the node self-latches (TSRAM-style).
why: Zero refresh power, with hold power ~0.05 pW/bit vs ~0.7 pW/bit for refresh today; the 60-75:1 capacitor module and its masks are replaced by low-AR epitaxy (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: Continuous-recharge Czochralski from PV: many ingots per crucible
idea: PV pullers grow 5-10 ingots per crucible by recharging granular polysilicon through a feed tube; adapt multi-recharge Cz, with devitrification-promoting crucible coatings for longer life, to 300 mm DRAM-grade wafers with in-line oxygen control.
why: High-purity quartz chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): crucible use per wafer down 3-5x and puller utilization up ~30%.

title: Anodic alumina pores on glass grow vertical access transistors
idea: Worse: pattern every vertical transistor with EUV contact holes. Flip: sputter aluminum on glass and anodize it into self-ordered 20-40 nm hexagonal pores. Fill the pores with ALD oxide-semiconductor channels wrapped by an ALD gate, giving vertical gate-all-around 4F2 access transistors with no transistor-level lithography.
why: Masks/EUV: removes the critical hole layer and reaches 4F2 density with low-capex anodization baths on glass.

title: Eliminate tungsten and its liner: barrierless molybdenum buried wordlines
idea: Fill buried-wordline trenches with molybdenum deposited by ALD/CVD directly on the gate dielectric with no TiN barrier, and spend the freed liner volume on conductor.
why: Scarce resource: swaps tungsten (China ~80%) for molybdenum mined in the US; removes a liner deposition per metallization and lowers wordline resistance ~30%, allowing thinner, easier wordlines.

title: Fully silicided polysilicon buried wordlines eliminate tungsten fill
idea: Ideal: wordlines that need no imported metal. Closest: fill the buried-wordline trench with in-situ-doped amorphous Si and fully convert it with a self-limiting Ni silicidation anneal (FUSI, as in fully silicided gates), skipping WF6 CVD, W etch-back and W CMP.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and Fact 4: removes W deposition tools and steps; NiSi ~15 uOhm-cm is competitive with thin W in narrow trenches.

title: Substitute oversized cell capacitors with power-up offset-trimmed sense amplifiers
idea: Store each sense amplifier's Vt-mismatch correction in a trimmed capacitor bank calibrated at power-up, so the bitline needs only ~25 mV of signal instead of 100+ mV; cells then need ~1-1.5 fF and bitline swing can be reduced.
why: Constraint: ~4x less cell charge plus reduced swing on shorter bitlines gives ~10x lower array energy per access; facet: capacitor AR from ~70:1 to ~20:1, shrinking the HAR etch/ALD module (fact 1).

title: Cell-pitch hybrid bonding of separate capacitor and transistor wafers
idea: Combine wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with the 1T1C cell: all capacitors are made on one wafer (free to use high thermal budget and high-k) and all access transistors on another. The wafers are bonded at ~40-60 nm pitch, and ~1% void-killed bonds are accepted as cell errors.
why: Each wafer flow sheds the other's constraints (~20% fewer steps, no capacitor-over-transistor thermal compromise), and the 1% budget makes sub-100 nm bonding yield-viable years earlier (facts 1, 2).

title: Joule self-heating crystallizes each tier's channel through its own wordline
idea: Effect: localized Joule heating. Deposit amorphous Si channels in every 3D DRAM tier, then send a microsecond current pulse through each lateral strip so only that strip melts and recrystallizes (self-aligned electrical annealing) while lower tiers and BEOL stay cold. A $1M program on 100 mm wafers with 4-tier stacks measures grain size and leakage in 24 months.
why: Fact 2: low-thermal-budget single-grain channels block 3D DRAM; pulse generators replace $10M+ excimer laser annealers.

title: 1D-only design rules: every critical layer is lines and cuts
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: make the cell tight in one direction only - active, wordline and bitline are pure line/space gratings by self-aligned quadruple patterning on DUV, all 2D information comes from cut masks at 3-4x pitch, and storage nodes are segments formed where two SAQP gratings intersect.
why: 1D gratings print on DUV at 20-24 nm pitch with high yield; removes EUV holes and pads (~5 EUV exposures) at ~10% cell-area penalty (fact 4).

title: Grow capacitor pillars upward by area-selective deposition
idea: Po: no etching, only growing. Pattern only tiny seed pads, then use area-selective deposition (inhibitor-blocked dielectric, nucleating metal) to grow TiN or Ru pillars straight up ~1 um, followed by conformal high-k and top plate: the capacitor is built additively, not dug.
why: High-AR etch capex and capacitor wall (fact 1): removes the 60-75:1 mold etch, the slowest and costliest module step; height no longer limited by etch bowing.

title: Moveable-type reticles: compose new periphery masks from tile library
idea: Borrowed from Gutenberg's moveable type: keep a library of reticles holding standard periphery 'glyphs' (sense-amp strip, row decoder, I/O cell, fuse bank), and a 10-person team writes the compositor that exposes each chip variant as a stitched multi-shot layout, so new DRAM organizations need zero new masks on non-array layers.
why: Facts 4/7: mask sets cost $5-15M and freeze designs; tile composition makes low-volume U.S. DRAM variants viable at a ~20-30% throughput cost on non-critical layers.

title: Block copolymer turns 180 nm trenches into 12 nm lines
idea: Inverts 'every line must be exposed'. Spin PS-b-PMMA into 180 nm stepper-defined trenches (graphoepitaxy), anneal so it self-assembles into ~12 nm lamellae aligned to the walls, remove the PMMA and transfer by RIE, a ~15x pitch multiplication from a hot plate.
why: Bitline/wordline gratings at modern pitch with 1990s steppers; materials cost cents per wafer (fact 4).

title: Fab federation chains depreciated 200 mm fabs into one line
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM line must be one site'. Assign each step block (front end, capacitor, BEOL, test) to one of a dozen fully depreciated U.S. 150/200 mm fabs, move wafers in sealed nitrogen-purged pods on scheduled trucks, and run one shared MES and yield database across them.
why: Uses capital already paid for (near-zero depreciation vs ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4); capacity in 12-18 months; U.S. manufacturability.

title: U.S. Memories redux: take-or-pay offtake with a price collar
idea: The 1989 U.S. Memories consortium (IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed before raising its ~$1B because DRAM prices fell and members refused binding purchase commitments. Fix exactly that: hyperscalers and OEMs sign 10-year take-or-pay contracts with a price collar (floor for lenders, ceiling for buyers in shortages like 2026) plus a federal buyer-of-last-resort backstop.
why: Capital intensity: investment-grade offtake cuts the fab's cost of capital from ~12% to ~6%, which on a wafer cost that is ~55% depreciation lowers cost per bit ~20-25% and makes a U.S. fab financeable.

title: Stiction-latched nanopillar relay built with the capacitor-hole etch
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: use the existing 70:1 mold etch to free-stand a ~20 nm TiN pillar between two side electrodes; a pull-in pulse snaps its tip onto one electrode where van der Waals adhesion (stiction, normally a yield killer) holds it at zero power, and the read senses which side conducts.
why: Zero refresh and zero standby; a ~1 um pillar resonates at ~20-50 MHz, giving ~10 ns switching; reuses DRAM's own HAR etch and ALD tools so conversion capex is small, with no dielectric-leakage spec at all (facts 3, 10).

title: Puff-pastry fold-and-bond doubles 3D DRAM tiers each round
idea: Fabricate one complete planar 1T1C tier on thinned donors, then laminate like croissant dough: bond tiers face-to-back in pairs, thin, bond pairs to pairs, so N tiers need only log2(N) sequential bond-thin rounds (5 rounds = 32 tiers) and every tier reuses the proven planar mask set; oversized landing pads absorb ~100 nm bond overlay.
why: Fact 2: reaches the ~26-tier break-even with planar-proven cells, sidestepping the lateral transistor and lateral capacitor; one identical tier flow runs at full volume.

title: Eliminate the ballroom cleanroom: wafers live inside a vacuum backbone
idea: Connect every process tool to a linear vacuum or nitrogen wafer highway so wafers never meet fab air from start to finish; the building becomes an ISO-8 warehouse without raised floors or giant make-up air handlers.
why: Capital and time: the cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction cost and a large energy share; could cut build time by about a year and total capex ~15%.

title: Vacuum-railway fab with no ballroom cleanroom
idea: Inverts 'a fab is a giant cleanroom building'. Link cluster tools with sealed sub-mTorr maglev tube conveyors so wafers never touch air from bare wafer to passivation; the building becomes an ordinary industrial shed with local maintenance enclosures.
why: Cleanroom shell, make-up air and HVAC are ~20-30% of a $15B fab and a large energy/water load; also removes queue-time oxidation limits.

title: 2050 engineer's cleanroom-less fab: wafers travel only in sealed tubes
idea: A 2050 engineer finds it odd that we filter a stadium of air to protect a 300 mm disc. Link conventional tools with a sealed pod-in-tube network held at vacuum or ultra-dry N2, with load-lock interfaces on every tool, so wafers never meet room air from start to finish and the building becomes a plain ISO-8 warehouse.
why: The ballroom cleanroom, make-up air and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction and a large energy load; removing them cuts build cost ~15-25% and build time. Risks: standardizing tool interfaces, and contamination inside the tubes.

title: Na: salt-hydrate thermal batteries shift heat rejection to night
idea: Store daytime chiller heat in sodium-sulfate-based salt-hydrate tanks tuned to melt near 30 C, then discharge overnight through dry coolers when ambient is lower, so the fab needs no evaporative cooling even in Arizona or Texas.
why: Water: makes dry cooling viable in U.S. Sun Belt fab clusters, cutting cooling water to ~0 without a heat-pump energy penalty.

title: Atomic steps on miscut wafers guide self-assembly
idea: Reverse the guide: use a deliberately miscut wafer whose annealed atomic step bunches form a natural periodic grating, which aligns block-copolymer self-assembly into cell lines with no litho template.
why: No EUV, no guide-pattern mask; pitch is set by the miscut angle and anneal, for near-zero litho cost on array layers.

title: Implant-free junctions from in-situ doped selective epitaxy
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: replace cell and periphery junction implants with in-situ doped selective epitaxy and conformal plasma doping, eliminating end-of-range implant damage that seeds trap-assisted gate-induced drain leakage at 125 C.
why: Facts 3 and 4: leakage tail tightened ~3x hot; removes ~6 implant steps and their masks and fewer high-current implanters.

title: Stack eight cheap wafers instead of shrinking one
idea: Rearrange density from the XY plane to the Z axis: build 2D DRAM arrays at a relaxed DUV pitch on 8 wafers and stack them wafer-on-wafer with hybrid bonding (no TSV), sharing one periphery wafer at the bottom.
why: No EUV; bit density per footprint ~4-6x a single relaxed die, and periphery is amortized over 8 array layers.

title: Decaffeination supercritical CO2: collapse-free drying for taller capacitors
idea: Adapt coffee decaffeination and supercritical extraction plants: after the wet etch that frees capacitor pillars, replace IPA drying with supercritical CO2 exchange (zero surface tension) so capillary forces never bend or stick pillars, letting aspect ratio climb toward 100-115:1 with fewer support layers.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) via yield: removes pattern collapse as the AR limit; claim +20-40% Cs headroom and fewer support-mesh deposition and etch steps.

title: Langmuir-Blodgett colloid monolayers pattern hexagonal capacitor arrays
idea: Revive Deckman's 1982 natural lithography and the 1930s Langmuir-Blodgett trough: transfer a wafer-scale monolayer of 30-40 nm silica spheres, steered into register by coarse imprinted wells over the landing pads, shrink the spheres by wet etch, evaporate a metal mesh and lift off to leave a hexagonal hole mask transferred by metal-assisted chemical etching. DRAM capacitors are already hexagonally packed, so the colloid matches the layout.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: replaces the SAQP or EUV step for DRAM's densest layer with a ~$1M trough and wet steps, with no excimer neon and no argon etch. Risk is colloid grain boundaries, handled by sizing arrays to domains and repairing vacancies with redundancy.

title: The mold is the electrode: keep a conductive mold
idea: Reverse mold-then-remove: etch capacitor holes into a conductive mold (doped poly-Si or TiN-rich stack) that stays in place as the outer plate, so you deposit only dielectric and inner electrode and skip mold strip and support-lattice formation.
why: Removes ~10-15% of capacitor-module steps (support mesh litho/etch, wet strip, collapse risk) at similar Cs.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor forming: anodically grown TiO2 dielectric that self-heals
idea: Electrolytic capacitors anodize ('form') their dielectric at a set voltage and 're-form' to heal weak spots; deposit a Ti/Al storage electrode, turn on every wordline so each cell is biased through its own access transistor, and anodize the electrode surface in a borate electrolyte to a voltage-set TiO2 thickness (~2 nm/V), re-forming after the crystallization anneal.
why: Hf/Ru-free dielectric without ALD (facts 1, 4): thickness is set by voltage, not precursor diffusion, so it is conformal at any AR; a wet bench costs ~10x less per pass than ALD; TiO2 k ~40-90.

title: Substitute sawn bulk wafers with reusable porous-silicon donor layer transfer
idea: Anodize a parent wafer to form a double porous-silicon release layer, grow 30-50 um of device-grade epitaxial silicon, bond it to a low-cost polysilicon carrier and split at the porous layer; the parent is re-polished and reused 20-50 times. DRAM front-end only needs the top few microns of single crystal.
why: Cuts ingot, polysilicon and quartz-crucible demand per DRAM wafer ~20x and lets U.S. epi reactors supply substrates.

title: Reusable parent wafer: porous-silicon layer transfer
idea: Minify Czochralski crystal use: grow a thin epitaxial silicon device layer on a porous-silicon release layer, transfer it to a cheap carrier, and reuse the parent wafer 50+ times.
why: Scarce resources: cuts high-purity quartz crucible and polysilicon demand (Spruce Pine chokepoint) per wafer by >90%.

title: Eliminate one-crystal-per-wafer: kerfless epitaxial lift-off from reusable parent wafers
idea: Grow a 50-100 um device-grade epitaxial silicon layer on a double-porous-silicon release layer atop a Czochralski parent wafer, bond it to a reclaimed-silicon carrier and cleave; the parent is re-porosified and reused 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resource and capital: cuts crystal pulls and high-purity quartz crucible consumption ~20x per wafer start, de-risking the Spruce Pine chokepoint; epi reactors are commodity, US-buildable tools.

title: Reusable donor wafers via porous-silicon release of device layers
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: only the top ~1 um needs device-grade crystal, so grow a double-porous Si release layer on a premium CZ donor, epi the device layer, bond it to a cheap reclaimed or multicrystalline handle, split at the porous layer and re-polish the donor for 10-20 reuses.
why: Cuts premium CZ wafer demand ~10x per bit, easing the Spruce Pine (>80%) quartz-crucible chokepoint, and gives a natural etch stop for backside processing (scarce resource, capital).

title: Reusable seed wafers via porous-silicon layer lift-off
idea: Po: the ingot needs no crucible. Grow device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer over a reusable seed wafer in existing epi reactors, bond the device layer to a cheap carrier and lift off, reusing the seed 10-20 times.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine quartz >80%): cuts Czochralski wafer demand ~5-10x per wafer start using existing epi capacity.

title: 2050 engineer's reusable parent wafer: kerfless porous-silicon lift-off
idea: A 2050 engineer laughs that we melt polysilicon in a quartz crucible and saw it for every slice. Grow DRAM-grade epitaxial silicon on a sintered double-layer porous-silicon release layer over a parent wafer, run the front end, bond the device layer to a cheap carrier, cleave at the porous layer, and re-polish the parent for ~10-20 more cycles.
why: Cuts prime-wafer and high-purity-quartz crucible demand ~10-20x (Spruce Pine chokepoint) and leaves a thin device layer ready for stacking. Risks: epi defects driving the retention tail, and porous-layer stability through 1000 C steps.

title: Crucible-free wafers: epitaxial lift-off from reusable seed wafers
idea: Constraint: no new high-purity quartz crucibles. Grow 20 um device-grade epi on a double-porous-silicon release layer, bond it to a polysilicon or SiC-ceramic handle, split it off, re-polish the seed and reuse it 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resource: cuts Czochralski crystal (and Spruce Pine crucible) demand >90%; wafer cost -30-50% at volume; epi reactors are U.S.-buildable.

title: Crystallographic KOH etching on (110) silicon for vertical trenches
idea: Revive 1970s anisotropic wet etching of (110) silicon, where KOH or TMAH attacks {110} ~100x faster than {111}, leaving atomically vertical {111} walls: align DRAM active-area and isolation trenches to <112> so a wet bath cuts 50:1 vertical walls with no plasma, using hard masks printed by LED or Talbot exposure. The crystal lattice becomes the CD reference.
why: Constraint and capital: replaces Ar/He-assisted STI and buried-wordline plasma etches with ~$1M wet benches; smooth {111} walls cut interface traps feeding the retention tail (Fact 3). Risks are a two-direction layout and lower nMOS mobility on (110).

title: Trench-capacitor eDRAM revived inside idle U.S. logic fabs
idea: Revive IBM/Siemens/Qimonda deep-trench DRAM, abandoned by commodity DRAM in 2009 but kept in IBM POWER eDRAM down to 14 nm: license the deep-trench module to U.S. logic fabs so they can sell multi-GB memory chiplets from idle 14-28 nm capacity. The trench is formed before transistors, so it fits logic flows without a dedicated DRAM line.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: no new fab dollars and only ~4 extra masks on depreciated 300 mm logic lines; trench Cs ~20-40 fF eases refresh; density is ~3-5x below 1-beta DRAM, so the gain is fast domestic supply at low marginal capex.

title: 1970s CCD memory flipped vertical inside a 3D NAND stack
idea: CCD memories (Intel 2416, Fairchild) died because serial shifting lost to DRAM's random access. Turn a 3D NAND stack into vertical CCD shift registers: 2-phase clock its 300 word-line layers to push 4-level charge packets along an IGZO channel whose low generation current preserves packets for seconds, with one sense amp per string top and no storage transistor or capacitor per bit.
why: Meets 100x: NAND fab cost structure with no per-bit device, 2 bits per packet; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: ~150 ns average shift latency for random words, best for streamed AI weights and KV pages.

title: Float-glass online APCVD: vacuum-free mold and interlayer oxides
idea: Float-glass lines coat moving ribbons at atmospheric pressure with SiO2 and SiOxCy; adapt gas-curtain-isolated atmospheric CVD heads (TEOS/ozone, silane/N2O) for DRAM's thick capacitor mold oxides, interlayer dielectrics and gap fills, with no vacuum chamber, load lock or turbo pump.
why: Tool capex and energy (fact 4): APCVD is ~1/3 the cost and footprint of PECVD per wafer-hour, and 1-2 um mold stacks are a heavy deposition load; Si, O, N, C, H only.

title: Eliminate CD-variation rework: per-bank voltage trims absorb multipatterning spread
idea: Instead of tightening process windows with more metrology, rework and scrap, trim each bank's VPP, VBLH and sense timing at sort so slow or leaky banks from DUV multipatterned arrays still meet JEDEC tRCD/tRAS and refresh specs. Host-visible timing is unchanged.
why: Allows looser overlay and CD specs (and so DUV instead of EUV) for a few trim fuses; estimated +5-10% yield and fewer inline metrology and rework passes.

title: Alien's question: grow memory tiers on the processor wafer's backside
idea: An alien asks why memory and compute come from different factories. After a GPU wafer finishes its front side and backside power network, deposit 4-16 tiers of <=400 C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell memory straight onto the backside, joined by nano-TSVs and built with the same backside tool set.
why: No separate memory wafer and no HBM stacking or interposer (facts 5, 6); wires ~10x shorter, maybe ~0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4, with memory capex riding on logic tools. High risk: hot logic below worsens retention.

title: Traffic light: three-wavelength resist prints three self-aligned levels per coat
idea: Random stimulus 'traffic light' (three colors, one pole) -> a resist with three photoacid systems is tuned to 365, 248 and 193 nm. One coat is exposed through three masks and developed once into three-level topography, which transfers into a self-aligned contact, bitline and landing pad sequence.
why: Process step count and capital (fact 4): coat/develop/etch loops fall up to 3x for stacked levels, and the levels are self-aligned by construction, so overlay errors between them disappear.

title: Transformer-coupled die stacking replaces TSVs, reviving IBM TROS
idea: Revive IBM's 1960s transformer read-only store, where data crossed between conductors by magnetic coupling, as inductive die-to-die links: each die in a DRAM stack carries top-metal coils that talk vertically through thinned silicon, so signals need no TSVs and power arrives by edge or wire bonds. Coils need no extra masks.
why: Fact 6: removes the TSV module (deep Si etch, liner, Cu fill, reveal; ~5-8 steps and a big yield hit) and TSV keep-out area, potentially halving HBM's area-per-bit penalty; risks are power delivery and coil area at 1-2 Tb/s per stack.

title: Wake-shield-inspired all-vacuum DRAM line with no cleanroom
idea: Extreme user: orbital fabs that get free ultra-high vacuum behind a wake shield. Recreate that on Earth by linking deposition, etch, anneal and (already-vacuum) EUV/e-beam tools through a continuous maglev vacuum wafer tunnel so wafers never touch air; the building drops to a gray corridor and native-oxide cleans vanish.
why: Capital/energy: cleanroom, HVAC and ultrapure-water plant are ~15-25% of fab capex and a large share of energy; also removes ~10% of clean/strip steps and shortens cycle time.

title: Bubble memory without garnet: field-driven skyrmion loops on glass
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (Intel Magnetics, TI) died on costly gadolinium gallium garnet substrates, bias magnets and slow propagation. Sputter Pt/Co/Ta skyrmion multilayers on glass or Si, keep bubble memory's global rotating in-plane field from a package coil to move every bit at once with no per-track drivers, and define tracks with one coarse imprint and one shared magnetoresistive sensor per major loop.
why: Meets 100x: no garnet and no per-bit transistor, just a film plus one pattern; est. ~$0.05-0.1/GB. Trades: us-level serial access, coil power.

title: Rotate the wafer, reuse one grating mask for wordlines and bitlines
idea: Rearrange the layout: design wordline and bitline layers as identical line/space gratings, and print both from the same reticle by rotating the wafer 90 degrees between the two exposures.
why: Fewer critical masks (one reticle for two layers), shared OPC and qualification; ~5-10% litho cost saving per generation.

title: Lensless interference lithography with 1990s excimer lasers
idea: Inverts 'lithography needs a lens and a mask'. Interfere two or three line-narrowed 248/193 nm excimer beams (Lloyd's-mirror geometry) at the wafer to expose ~110-130 nm-pitch gratings or hexagonal arrays over a whole 200 mm wafer in one flash, then halve with one spacer step.
why: A ~$1M optical bench replaces a $100M+ scanner for every periodic array layer (fact 4); coherence over full-wafer area is the risk.

title: Lloyd's-mirror crossed interference exposures print maskless pillar lattices
idea: Box: Si charge x vertical pillar transistor x standard sensing x 2D x Si x 266/325 nm laser Lloyd's-mirror interference lithography, two exposures at 90 degrees. Interference fringes print a perfectly periodic dot lattice over the wafer in seconds with no mask, and array-edge cuts plus periphery are added with a contact-aligner exposure.
why: Mask and EUV dependence for periodic arrays: a ~$50k optical table vs a $150M+ scanner; 100-150 nm pitch today, path below 40 nm with 193 nm immersion interference; risk is overlay of later layers to the lattice.

title: Solid-state laser interference prints 38 nm half-pitch gratings on a benchtop
idea: Effect: two-beam optical interference. Build an immersion Lloyd's-mirror interferometer with a ~$120k 213 nm fifth-harmonic Nd:YAG and a high-index prism; the fringes give about 38 nm half-pitch over a cm2 field, stepped and stitched across 100 mm wafers, and a double exposure at 60 degrees gives honeycomb arrays. $1M covers optics, resist and university fab access.
why: Fact 4: shows array layers can be printed by a <$300k tool, the first step toward a dedicated interference array-layer printer for U.S. fabs.

title: Substitute one-bit cells with analog charge levels and charge-domain MAC
idea: Use larger DUV-defined capacitors (~4x area, no EUV) holding 16 charge levels (4 bits) for AI weights or KV cache; on access, selected cells dump charge onto a summing line weighted by input voltages, so a whole dot product is read with one ADC conversion instead of streaming every bit out.
why: Constraint: one result moves instead of N operands, ~10-50x lower energy per MAC-equivalent access; facet: equal bit density with ~2x coarser lithography and no EUV.

title: Elapsed-time-aware sensing reads decayed charge without refresh
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: instead of holding charge constant, make the read reference follow it - each row stores a few-bit write-epoch tag, and the sense reference is stepped down along the measured decay of matched reference cells written at the same time, keeping cells readable ~10x longer; paired with a page time-to-live, refresh is never issued.
why: Zero refresh; ~10x usable retention lets the fab cut Cs or accept a leakier, cheaper access transistor (drop a halo/channel implant mask, shallower buried gate) (facts 3, 4).

title: Retired 3D NAND lines prototype 3D DRAM via replacement-gate recess
idea: Po: a NAND fab is a DRAM fab. Older 64/96-layer 3D NAND lines already run oxide/nitride stacks, high-AR hole etch, lateral nitride recess and metal fill; reuse that replacement-gate recess to carve lateral capacitor cavities and channel slots for horizontal-cell 3D DRAM, filling with Mo instead of W.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM yet (fact 2): paid-off tools already proven beyond 26 tiers; no new fab and less tungsten.

title: S: sublimable sulfur scaffolds support tall structures, then vanish
idea: Fill cavities and slits with molten elemental sulfur (melts ~115 C) as a temporary mechanical support and planarizer during subsequent steps, then sublime it away in vacuum at ~150-200 C, leaving clean cavities.
why: Water: replaces sacrificial-oxide fill plus wet strip and rinse in 3D-DRAM and capacitor flows (~100% water cut for the module), and props very tall stacks against collapse.

title: Erasure-coded HBM stacks built from barely tested dies
idea: Combine storage-array Reed-Solomon erasure coding with HBM stacking: 12+2 dies are stacked with only a gross-short screen, and each line is striped across dies with RS(14,12). Up to two dead dies plus 1% cell errors per die are tolerated.
why: HBM stack yield is down 20-30% and pre-stack known-good-die test is costly (fact 6). Erasure coding raises stack yield toward ~99% and removes most pre-stack test.

title: MITI 3D-IC laser recrystallization stacks single-crystal DRAM tiers
idea: Revive Japan's 1981-90 MITI 3D-IC programme, which made stacked single-crystal silicon by laser zone-melting through seed windows: deposit amorphous silicon for each 3D-DRAM tier and melt it with a scanned green Nd:YVO4 solid-state laser (no excimer, no neon) so it regrows epitaxially from seed holes to the tier below, giving crystalline lateral access transistors tier by tier.
why: Fact 2: single-crystal lateral transistors without a thick Si/SiGe superlattice epi and its thermal budget; solid-state lasers cost ~$1-3M and need no rare gas. Risks are heat reaching lower tiers and grain boundaries far from seeds.

title: Laser-grown single-grain silicon tiers stacked over finished arrays
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must live in the wafer'. Deposit a-Si over the previous tier, etch 180 nm grain-filter holes, and melt it with a 1990s XeCl excimer pulse so each transistor sits in one location-controlled grain (micro-Czochralski), then repeat for 8-16 tiers below a 450 C substrate budget.
why: Monolithic 3D without bonding or epi, with one cheap mask set reused per tier (facts 2, 4); grain-boundary-free channels keep leakage near bulk.

title: Micro-Czochralski laser seeds: one window mask grows tier crystals
idea: Open seed holes with the one added mask in the inter-tier oxide, deposit amorphous Si above, and melt it with an excimer laser so each hole bottom acts as a tiny Czochralski seed and grain filter, recrystallizing one location-controlled single-crystal grain per array tile for the next tier's access transistors.
why: Fact 2: monolithic stacked tiers with near-single-crystal mobility and a tighter leakage tail, without bonding tools or epi superlattices.

title: Sixteen layer-transferred DUV tiers replace EUV shrink for density
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation moves density into height: transfer a ~50 nm single-crystal Si film per tier by smart-cut, build only an ~8-mask DUV array tier of planar nonvolatile cells (e.g., 6F2 at F~40 nm with asymmetric-electrode AFE capacitors) at <=500 C with laser dopant activation, and repeat 16 times above one shared periphery.
why: Zero refresh; 16 tiers at ~0.0096 um2/bit give ~0.0006 um2/bit effective, beating 1b-node DRAM (~0.00086) with zero EUV; capex shifts from scanners to cheap repeated DUV and bonding modules (facts 2, 4).

title: Moire-fringe overlay upgrade lets used contact aligners reach 5 nm alignment
idea: Effect: moire magnification. Pairs of slightly mismatched gratings on mask and wafer produce fringes that magnify misalignment ~1000x; a $5k camera reads them and drives a closed-loop piezo stage retrofitted to a ~$100k used proximity aligner or imprint tool, giving sub-5 nm overlay for array layers. $1M funds two retrofits and 24 months of overlay qualification.
why: Fact 4: overlay is the barrier to cheap patterning; ~$250k per tool versus $50-200M scanners.

title: Matryoshka multi-shell capacitor contacted by etch-selective recesses
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting resolves 'more charge but no taller hole': ALD alternating TiN and Ru electrode shells separated by ZrO2 inside one hole, then a TiN-selective top recess and a Ru-selective bottom recess tie odd shells to the storage node and even shells to the plate, giving 3-4 parallel capacitor walls per hole.
why: Cs ~2-2.5x per hole at constant AR, so today's ~5 fF needs only ~30:1 instead of 60-75:1; removes 1-2 support-mesh masks and the slowest HAR etch tool-hours (facts 1, 4).

title: MLCC-in-a-hole: interleaved multi-electrode capacitor at low aspect ratio
idea: Borrowed from multilayer ceramic capacitors, which reach uF by stacking hundreds of interleaved electrodes: in a wider, shallower storage hole (AR ~20) ALD 4-6 alternating TiN/ZrO2 shells, then tie odd shells together at the bottom and even shells at the top with selective recess-and-cap, so capacitance multiplies with the number of dielectric layers.
why: Facts 1/4: 3-4x Cs per footprint without going to AR 115, relaxing the hardest etch; selective alternate-electrode contacting is the risky step.

title: Eliminate idle EUV capex: national EUV pass utility shared by memory makers
idea: A government-backed consortium owns EUV scanners in one US litho hall beside several fabs and sells exposure passes; FOUPs move by sealed AMHS tunnel between companies, so no DRAM maker buys a full EUV fleet. Products remain standard DDR5/HBM.
why: Capital: lifts EUV utilization from ~60-70% to >90% across companies and lets new US entrants pay per exposure, cutting entry capex by billions.

title: H: remote atomic-hydrogen pre-clean replaces RCA wet benches
idea: Remove native oxide, carbon and metal-organic residue before epi and gate steps with remote atomic hydrogen at 300-500 C plus NF3/NH3 radical oxide removal in the same vacuum cluster, so wafers go from etch to deposition without a wet bench.
why: Water: RCA-type cleans are the largest category of UPW use; a dry pre-clean cuts it >10x and frees bench floor space.

title: Mg: magnesiothermic reduction turns stubby oxide posts into porous capacitors
idea: Pattern short SiO2 posts (AR ~15), expose them to Mg vapor at ~650 C so SiO2 + 2Mg -> Si + 2MgO forms a nanoporous Si sponge, strip the MgO, then coat with ALD dielectric and electrode; surface area rises ~10x without a high-aspect-ratio etch.
why: Fact 1: decouples capacitance from aspect ratio, so the 60-75:1 etch (the costliest capacitor step) shrinks to ~15:1 or Cs rises several-fold at the same height.

title: Revive BST, the abandoned gigabit-era DRAM dielectric, by N2-ALD
idea: Revive (Ba,Sr)TiO3, the k~200-300 perovskite the 1990s gigabit DRAM programmes abandoned because it could not be deposited conformally: grow it by ALD with nitrogen purge and ozone, crystallize it with a solid-state-laser spike anneal instead of a xenon flash lamp, and use SrRuO3 electrodes to suppress the interfacial dead layer. An effective k of 70-100 at 8 nm already meets Fact 1's target.
why: Fact 1 and capital: k ~70+ lets the capacitor drop from AR 60-75 to ~30, halving the hardest etch time, easing pattern collapse and deleting support-lattice steps. Risks are thin-film leakage and thermal budget.

title: Cold repeated ion-cut tier stacking with microwave dopant activation
idea: Box: gain-cell or capacitor charge x planar single-crystal Si transistor per tier x standard sensing x 8-16 tiers via layer transfer x Si x hydrogen ion-cut plus microwave anneal below 450 C. Each tier is a single-crystal film transferred from a reusable donor onto the previous patterned tier, exposed with the same DUV masks, and activated by microwaves that couple to dopants without cooking lower tiers.
why: 3D DRAM manufacturability (fact 2) with single-crystal channels and reused masks, so bits/area scale with tiers at flat mask count; risk is per-tier yield and reaching the ~26-tier break-even.

title: Canon ELTRAN porous-silicon transfer builds 30-tier single-crystal 3D DRAM
idea: Canon's ELTRAN layer transfer (epitaxy on porous Si, split by water jet) lost to Smart Cut on cost for single SOI layers. For 3D DRAM needing 26+ single-crystal tiers its advantage returns: one donor is re-epitaxied and split repeatedly, each tier bonded below 400 C onto the growing stack with one coarse alignment litho per tier and no hydrogen implant.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): supplies single-crystal lateral-transistor tiers without Si/SiGe superlattice limits; donor reused ~50x; per-tier cost ~one bond plus split.

title: Planed wood-grain staircase: one sloped trough exposes every tier
idea: Use the single added mask to open a wide trough at the array edge and etch it through reflowed resist into a 5-10 degree ramp; deposit the tier stack conformally, then CMP flat so each tier surfaces as its own ~400 nm stripe, like grain on a planed board, giving wordline contact landings for all tiers.
why: Capital/throughput: replaces the multi-mask staircase with dozens of trim-etch loops by one mask plus one CMP for 3D DRAM.

title: Si: vicinal-wafer atomic step bunches as maskless wordline template
idea: Cut Si(111) wafers at a precise miscut so a UHV/H2 anneal bunches atomic steps into a self-ordered array whose pitch is set by the miscut angle (e.g. 24 nm); selectively nucleate an oxide or metal along the step edges to form the dense wordline hardmask with no exposure at all for that array layer.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): the crystal lattice becomes the ruler, deleting one EUV or SAQP line layer (~4-8 steps) in the array; ~3-5% wafer-cost cut if edge-roughness is controllable.

title: Tree rings: magnetic racetrack on vertical hole walls, one litho layer
idea: Random stimulus 'tree rings' (records stored along depth) -> a perpendicular magnetic multilayer is deposited conformally on the sidewall of each NAND-like vertical hole, and bits are stored as domains along the depth, shifted by current pulses to a read/write MTJ at the top. One hole lithography defines 32-128 bits.
why: Non-volatile, with unlimited domain-wall-shift endurance. Bits per litho step rise ~50x, which collapses mask and EUV cost per bit; access is ~20-80 ns.

title: Rent idle U.S. logic back-end lines for monolithic memory layers
idea: Turn spare back-end-of-line capacity at U.S. logic fabs into memory capacity: after the logic interconnect, add 6-10 oxide-semiconductor gain-cell layers at <400 C using existing BEOL tools and ArF litho, so memory rides on logic wafers already in production.
why: Near-zero new capex adds supply without a DRAM fab; memory directly above compute cuts data movement (Fact 5).

title: Antiferroelectric zirconia capacitors store more charge using existing tools
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: tune the ZrO2 already used in DRAM capacitors into a dopant-stabilized antiferroelectric phase with asymmetric electrodes, so the built-in bias parks the cell on the steep field-induced transition and the effective k in the sensing window exceeds ~100 from -40 to 125 C.
why: Facts 1 and 4: same ALD and etch tools, but ~2x charge per area lets capacitor AR fall from ~70 to ~40, cutting etch time and hardmask steps.

title: Integrated-passive-device fabs supply ready-made trench capacitor wafers
idea: Borrowed from smartphone silicon capacitors (IPD trench caps, ~1 pF/um2) made in old 200 mm fabs: a 10-person team designs a cell-pitch trench-capacitor array, buys the wafers from an IPD foundry, buys transistor wafers from a foundry shuttle and has an OSAT hybrid-bond them; the team owns only design, integration and test.
why: Facts 1/3: at ~0.5 um pitch each cell gets ~100+ fF, enough for near-refresh-free retention or 3-bit multilevel storage; density is far below commodity DRAM, so it targets low-refresh, U.S.-made niche memory with zero fab capex.

title: Diatom polyamine emulsions grow capacitor silica molds without lithography
idea: Diatoms build frustule pores by letting phase-separated polyamine droplets template silica precipitation; spin a long-chain polyamine/phosphate film that breaks into droplets pinned on each hydrophilic storage-node landing pad, then feed silicic acid so silica grows only in the continuous phase. Burning out the organics leaves a self-registered honeycomb mold of deep pores for the cylinder capacitor.
why: Deletes the capacitor-mold exposure, its hardmask stack and the 60-75:1 plasma etch (facts 1, 4) with a room-temperature wet step; est. one fewer critical litho layer and 8-12% lower wafer cost.

title: Green-building LEED rating applied to memory supply chains
idea: LEED made builders compete on green features; create a 'chokepoint-free memory' rating that scores DRAM by banned-element content (Hf, Ru, Co, W, Ta, In, Ga), helium use and quartz source, and tie federal and hyperscaler purchase preference and accelerated depreciation to higher grades.
why: Policy for capital and resilience: a premium market repays R&D on abundant-element processes and shields U.S. fabs from W and Ga export controls.

title: Eliminate helium from the fab: hydrogen backside cooling and tracer leak checks
idea: Replace helium backside gas on etch and CVD electrostatic chucks with low-pressure hydrogen or forming gas (higher thermal conductivity, sealed with flow monitoring), and replace helium mass-spec leak checks with 5% hydrogen tracer detection.
why: Scarce resource: Qatar's ~30% helium share is offline; fab helium use could drop >80%, removing a supply shock that can idle etch fleets.

title: Glass-lid wafer-level package: hermetic, polymer-free, sealed before dicing
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years with zero polymers: direct-bond a borosilicate lid wafer carrying through-glass vias onto the finished DRAM wafer at low temperature, forming a hermetic chip-scale package before dicing with solder-free Cu pillar outputs.
why: Packaging capital and reliability: removes molding, underfill and organic-substrate steps (~-30% package cost) and the humidity/ionic failure modes that dominate at 125 C.

title: Bottom-up VLS-grown vertical nanowire access transistors on landing pads
idea: Box: Si capacitor charge x vertical gate-all-around Si nanowire grown, not etched x voltage sense amp x capacitor-over-transistor x Si x vapor-liquid-solid growth from Al or Sn catalyst dots placed by electroless self-aligned deposition on bitline contacts. ALD then wraps the gate and a spacer etch forms wordlines, giving a 4F2 vertical cell without an EUV pillar exposure.
why: Litho capital (fact 4) and density: removes 1-2 EUV layers and the pillar etch while enabling 4F2 (~33% smaller than 6F2); risk is catalyst contamination, growth-direction yield and diameter uniformity.

title: Titanium-industry cold crucibles: quartz-free Czochralski silicon
idea: Titanium and multicrystalline-silicon casting melt the charge inside water-cooled segmented copper 'cold crucibles' where induction fields hold the melt off the wall; adapt a cold-crucible induction Czochralski puller to 300 mm DRAM ingots, metering oxygen through a controlled SiO feed to keep the interstitial oxygen needed for gettering.
why: High-purity quartz chokepoint (Spruce Pine >80%): eliminates quartz crucibles entirely with only Cu and Si, and lowers crucible-dissolution contamination.

title: Skull-melt crystal growth: silicon is its own crucible
idea: Reverse the container: use cold-crucible induction melting where a water-cooled segmented copper cage keeps a frozen silicon skull that holds the melt, so no high-purity quartz crucible is needed for Czochralski pulling.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint (>80% share) and cuts oxygen in the wafers, which may shorten the leakage tail.

title: Cubic-zirconia skull melting: silicon grown inside its own frozen crust
idea: Borrowed from cubic-zirconia growth, where an RF-heated melt freezes against water-cooled copper fingers into its own container skin: apply cold-crucible induction melting to silicon crystal pulling, so a silicon skull holds the melt and no fused-quartz crucible is used.
why: Scarce resource: removes >80% Spruce Pine dependence; less oxygen in the crystal may also trim leakage-tail defects (Fact 3). Thermal-gradient control for 300 mm dislocation-free growth is the risk.

title: Crucible-free silicon via cold-crucible induction Czochralski
idea: Inverts 'silicon crystals grow from quartz crucibles'. Melt Si in a segmented water-cooled copper crucible where electromagnetic pressure and a solid Si skull keep the melt off the walls, and pull 300 mm crystals with no high-purity quartz.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine >80% quartz chokepoint; lower oxygen content may also tighten the retention tail (fact 3).

title: Cold-crucible induction Czochralski growth eliminates high-purity quartz crucibles
idea: Edge case borrowed from microgravity float-zone growth, where the melt touches nothing. Melt silicon in a segmented water-cooled copper crucible with induction heating so a frozen silicon skull contains the melt, and pull 300 mm ingots without Spruce Pine quartz.
why: Scarce resource: removes the >80% Spruce Pine crucible chokepoint and lowers oxygen in the wafer, which also helps retention.

title: Electromagnetic cold-crucible Czochralski eliminates Spruce Pine quartz crucibles
idea: Effect: Lorentz-force melt levitation (cold-crucible induction). Grow 300 mm Si boules from a segmented water-cooled copper crucible in which high-frequency eddy currents hold the melt off the walls, while a cusp magnetic field damps convection. Oxygen for gettering comes from a small consumable silica rod instead of a full crucible.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint: Spruce Pine supplies >80% of HP quartz crucibles; this removes that dependency and the crucible consumable cost.

title: Substitute dissipative line charging with adiabatic resonant charge recovery
idea: Drive bitline precharge and wordlines from LC resonant rails using high-Q spiral inductors in a thick-copper redistribution layer borrowed from RF BEOL, ramping lines over ~5 ns so most of their CV2 energy returns to the tank instead of heating drivers.
why: Constraint: adiabatic recovery of 80-90% of line energy gives ~5-10x per access on the dominant line-charging term; facet: no new array lithography, only one mature thick-metal layer.

title: MicroLED mass transfer: stamp-printed DRAM dielets onto logic wafers
idea: Borrowed from microLED displays, which move millions of 10 um LEDs at once with elastomer stamps: make 100x100 um DRAM array dielets on cheap mature-node wafers, undercut-release them, and transfer-print hundreds per die directly onto accelerator wafers beside the compute, wired with one redistribution layer.
why: Facts 5/6: near-memory without TSVs or HBM stacks; only known-good dielets get printed, lifting yield; transfer-print tools cost ~$5M versus TSV lines.

title: Catt-spiral wafer-scale DRAM that routes around bad tiles
idea: Revive Anamartic's 1989 Wafer Stack, built on Ivor Catt's self-organizing spiral: every DRAM tile on an uncut wafer tests itself at power-up and links to a good neighbour, forming a chain that skips bad tiles, while a wafer-level redistribution layer brings out wide buses to a host. No dicing, die test, packaging or TSVs.
why: Fact 6 and capital: avoids HBM's ~3x area-per-bit TSV tax and 20-30% stack yield loss plus packaging and test lines (~15-25% of DRAM cost); tolerates lower yield, so depreciated 300 mm lines can make bandwidth-rich memory.

title: Edge-face interconnect stacking instead of through-silicon vias
idea: Po: the wiring goes around, not through. Stack thinned DRAM dies, polish one side of the stack, route every die's I/O to that side face, and lithograph a redistribution layer there that hybrid-bonds to a logic die standing perpendicular to the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out area and TSV-yield loss, recovering ~10-20% area per bit and much of the 20-30% stack yield loss.

title: Sticker-book kid: micro-transfer-print periphery chiplets onto low-T arrays
idea: A kid peels finished stickers onto a page. Make sense-amp and decoder chiplets (~100x100 um) in a cheap mature CMOS fab, release them by undercut, pick thousands at once with an elastomer stamp using kinetic adhesion, and print them onto the <=400 C memory-array wafer or panel, wired by one BEOL redistribution layer; the memory fab itself never exceeds 400 C.
why: Splits the high-temperature periphery (49% of die) from the low-temperature arrays so each runs on its cheapest line; one stamp moves ~10k chiplets per cycle. Risk: ~1 um placement accuracy limits connection density.
